## Activation functions

After each layer of a neural network, every neuron passes its result through an **activation function** — a simple rule that decides how strong the neuron's output signal should be.

Without activation functions, stacking many layers would still be mathematically equivalent to a single **linear transformation** (a straight-line rule). It is the **non-linear** activation between layers that lets a deep network learn curved, complex **decision boundaries** — the shapes that separate different categories in the data.

### Two common activation functions

**ReLU (rectified linear unit)** is the simplest: it passes positive values through unchanged and turns any negative value into zero. Think of it as a gate that opens for positive signals and closes completely for negative ones.

**Sigmoid** squeezes any value into a **bounded range** between zero and one, producing an S-shaped output. This is useful when you want the output to look like a probability.

### Why non-linearity matters

Imagine trying to draw a curved boundary between two groups of points using only a ruler. A purely **linear** layer cannot do this. Stack as many linear layers as you like — the result is still one straight-line rule. Adding a **non-linear** activation function after each layer gives the network the power to bend and curve, which is essential for solving real-world problems.
